entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11898"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 47</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:1-23</reference>. Vision of the Temple Waters. Borders and Division of The land.</title> <div sID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> The happy fruit to the earth at large of God's dwelling with Israel in holy fellowship is that the blessing is no longer restricted to the one people and locality, but is to be diffused with comprehensive catholicity through the whole world. So the plant from the cedar of Lebanon is represented as gathering under its shelter "all fowl of every wing" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>). Even the desert places of the earth shall be made fruitful by the healing waters of the Gospel (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Is 35:1</reference>).<div eID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11898"/><hi type="bold">1. waters--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>, represents "the water of life as proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." His throne was set up in the temple at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>). Thence it is to flow over the earth (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">14:8</reference>). Messiah is the temple and the door; from His pierced side flow the living waters, ever increasing, both in the individual believer and in the heart. The fountains in the vicinity of Moriah suggested the image here. The waters flow eastward, that is, towards the Kedron, and thence towards the Jordan, and so along the Ghor into the Dead Sea. The main point in the picture is the rapid augmentation from a petty stream into a mighty river, not by the influx of side streams, but by its own self-supply from the sacred miraculous source in the temple [Henderson]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">46:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>). Searching into the things of God, we find some easy to understand, as the water up to the ankles; others more difficult, which require a deeper search, as the waters up to the knees or loins; others beyond our reach, of which we can only adore the depth (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>). The healing of the waters of the Dead Sea here answers to "there shall be no more curse" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.11">Zec 14:11</reference>). <div eID="gen21494" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 47 Eze 47:1-23 . Vision of the Temple Waters. Borders and Division of The land. Even the desert places of the earth shall be made fruitful by the healing waters of the Gospel (compare Is 35:1 ). 1. waters-- So Re 22:1 , represents "the water of life as proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." His throne was set up in the temple at Jerusalem ( Eze 43:7 ). Thence it is to flow over the earth ( Joe 3:18 ; Zec 13:1 ; 14:8 ). Messiah is the temple and the door; from His pierced side flow the living waters, ever increasing, both in the individual believer and in the heart. The fountains in the vicinity of Moriah suggested the image here. The waters flow eastward, that is, towards the Kedron, and thence towards the Jordan, and so along the Ghor into the Dead Sea. The main point in the picture is the rapid augmentation from a petty stream into a mighty river, not by the influx of side streams, but by its own self-supply from the sacred miraculous source in the temple [Henderson]. The healing of the waters of the Dead Sea here answers to "there shall be no more curse" ( Re 22:3 ; compare Zec 14:11 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11900"/><div sID="gen21496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11900"/><hi type="bold">8. the desert--</hi>or "plain," Hebrew, Arabah (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">De 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.49">4:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos 3:16</reference>), which is the name still given to the valley of the Jordan and the plain south of the Dead Sea, and extending to the Elanitic gulf of the Red Sea.<div eID="gen21496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sea--</hi>the Dead Sea. "The sea" noted as covering with its waters the guilty cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah. In its bituminous waters no vegetable or animal life is said to be found. But now death is to give place to life in Judea, and throughout the world, as symbolized by the healing of these death-pervaded waters covering the doomed cities. Compare as to "the sea" in general, regarded as a symbol of the troubled powers of nature, disordered by the fall, henceforth to rage no more, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>. <div eID="gen21497" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11901"/><div sID="gen21498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11901"/><hi type="bold">9. rivers--</hi>in Hebrew, "two rivers." Hence Hebrew expositors think that the waters from the temple were divided into two branches, the one emptying itself into the eastern or Dead Sea, the other into the western or Mediterranean. So <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>. However, though this probably is covertly implied in the Hebrew dual, the flowing of the waters into the Dead Sea only is expressed. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">Eze 47:8</reference>, "waters ... healed," which can apply only to it, not to the Mediterranean: also <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>, "fish as the fish of the great sea"; the Dead Sea, when healed, containing fish, as the Mediterranean does. <div eID="gen21498" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11902"/><div sID="gen21499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11902"/><hi type="bold">10. En-gedi ... En-eglaim--</hi>En-gedi (meaning "fountain of the kid"), anciently, Hazazon-Tamar, now Ain-Jidy; west of the Dead Sea; David's place of refuge from Saul. En-eglaim means "fountain of two calves," on the confines of Moab, over against En-gedi, and near where Jordan enters the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">Is 15:8</reference>). These two limits are fixed on, to comprise between them the whole Dead Sea.<div eID="gen21499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fish ... according to their kinds--</hi>Jerome quotes an ancient theory that "there are a hundred fifty-three kinds of fishes," all of which were taken by the apostles (<reference osisRef="John.21.11">Joh 21:11</reference>), and not one remained uncaptured; signifying that both the noble and baseborn, the rich and the poor, and every class, are being drawn out of the sea of the world to salvation. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.47">Mt 13:47</reference>, the gospel net; the apostles being fishermen, at first literally, afterwards spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.19">Mt 4:19</reference>). <div eID="gen21500" type="x-p"/>

The redivision of the land: the boundaries. The latter are substantially the same as those given by Moses in <reference osisRef="Num.34.1-Num.34.29">Nu 34:1-29</reference>; they here begin with the north, but in Numbers they begin with the south (<reference osisRef="Num.34.3">Nu 34:3</reference>). It is only Canaan proper, exclusive of the possession of the two and a half tribes beyond Jordan, that is here divided.<div eID="gen21506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joseph ... two portions--</hi>according to the original promise of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.5">Ge 48:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">22</reference>). Joseph's sons were given the birthright forfeited by Reuben, the first-born (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>). Therefore the former is here put first. His two sons having distinct portions make up the whole number twelve portions, as he had just before specified "twelve tribes of Israel"; for Levi had no separate inheritance, so that he is not reckoned in the twelve. <div eID="gen21507" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11907"/><div sID="gen21509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11907"/><hi type="bold">16. Hamath--</hi>As Israel was a separate people, so their land was a separate land. On no scene could the sacred history have been so well transacted as on it. On the east was the sandy desert. On the north and south, mountains. On the west, an inhospitable sea-shore. But it was not always to be a separate land. Between the parallel ranges of Lebanon is the long valley of El-Bekaa, leading to "the entering in of Hamath" on the Orontes, in the Syrian frontier. Roman roads, and the harbor made at Cæsarea, opened out doors through which the Gospel should go from it to all lands. So in the last days, when all shall flock to Jerusalem as the religious center of the world.<div eID="gen21509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Berothah--</hi>a city in Syria conquered by David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.8">2Sa 8:8</reference>); meaning "wells."<div eID="gen21510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hazar-hatticon--</hi>meaning "the middle village."<div eID="gen21511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hauran--</hi>a tract in Syria, south of Damascus; Auranitis. <div eID="gen21512" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11911"/><div sID="gen21516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11911"/><hi type="bold">22. to the strangers--</hi>It is altogether unprecedented under the old covenant, that "strangers" should have "inheritance" among the tribes. There would not be room locally within Canaan for more than the tribes. The literal sense must therefore be modified, as expressing that Gentiles are not to be excluded from settling among the covenant-people, and that spiritually their privileges are not to be less than those of Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.12">Ro 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">10</reference>). Still, "sojourneth," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:23</reference>, implies that in Canaan, the covenant people are regarded as at home, the strangers as settlers. <chapter eID="Ezek.47"/>
entries.content_plain: 22. to the strangers-- It is altogether unprecedented under the old covenant, that "strangers" should have "inheritance" among the tribes. Still, "sojourneth," in Eze 47:23 , implies that in Canaan, the covenant people are regarded as at home, the strangers as settlers.
